newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: HOWARD ATTACKS ASIAN NEWSPAPERS
The Prime Minister says some sections of the Asian media have written in ignorance of what he has said about racism.
Asian newspapers have criticised the stance Mr Howard has taken in the race debate.
But the Prime Minister says he has never been and will never be reluctant to repudiate racism.
He's told Parliament he has repeatedly denounced racism, praised the contribution of Asian immigrants and stated a commitment to a non-discriminatory immigration policy.
Mr Howard says suggestions in some sections of the Asian media that he has encouraged any acts of discrimination against Asian Australians are absolutely wrong.
CALL FOR WAGE RESTRAINT AT TOP LEVELS
Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, has called for wage restraint from executives as well as employees.
He has said there should be more moderate wage claims because inflation is low.
The Treasurer has told a Coalition party meeting employees can't be expected to exercise restraint if managers don't.
QLD COMMISSIONER QUITS
In a dramatic development in Brisbane, the Commissioner who headed up an inquiry into the Coalition's Memorandum of Understanding with the Police Union has quit.
His resignation is immediate.

Kenneth Carruthers, QC, says his ability to pursue the matter independently and impartially had been taken from him because of threats arising from an inquiry set up into the conduct of the Criminal Justice Commission.
He said the Premier Rob Borbidge and Police Minister, Russell Cooper, are members of the government which established the Connolly Ryan Inquiry, which is now investigating his own inquiry.
Mr Carruthers says lawyers for the Connolly Ryan Inquiry told him he'd have to produce all notes and written documents in relation to his inquiry into the Memorandum of Understanding.
RACISM INGRAINED-STUDY
A new report on racism says to deny Australia's racist history or to deny racism, is to be part of it.
Sue Zelinka of the Human Rights Commission makes the observation in a report entitled Understanding Racism in Australia.
Ms Zelinka says racism has beem deeply ingrained in Australian history since colonisation.
She has identified several types of racism, from singling out an individual or group for racist behaviour, to institutional racism.
Ms Zelinka says there's also indirect racism where a group is not identified by name.
BLACKHAWK INQUIRY HEARS GRAPHIC ACCOUNT
A ground technician has told the Blackhawk inquiry in Townsville he saw the mid-air collision between two helicopters in June.
The Board of Inquiry is investigating the night-time collision in which 18 servicemen died during a counter terrorism exercise.
Lance corporal Keven Meddings said he saw Blackhawk Two flying straight ahead silhouetted against the sky then the rotor disk of another helicopter.
He heard a bang and saw the blades cut into the tail boom of Blakhawk Two, then the rear aircraft exploded and burst into flames.
SUPREME COURT RULES ON PYRAMID SHARES
The Supreme Court has ruled holders of non-withdrawable Pyramid shares will not be treated like depositors.
The shareholders say although this is a major setback they will fight to prove the shares were never valid...and they deserve their money back just like any other creditor.
Nearly 5000 investors are seeking to recover 87-million-dollars lost in the collapse of the Pyramid group of building societies.
The trial is expected to resume in a couple of weeks.
WOMAN ATTACKED BY ROGUE BUFFALO
In the Northern Territory, a 48 year-old woman is recovering in Royal Darwin Hospital after being attacked by a rogue buffalo.
A large mature bull with fully developed horns gored the woman's leg, and knocked her off the bonnet of her car causing her to break her arm.
She's also suffering head injuries, but is in a stable condition.
The incident happened at a water hole near Katherine south east of Darwin.
SUPERLEAGUE REJECTS QUESTIONS ON ITS ABILITY
Reports that a British Lions tour of the Pacific is falling apart because of a lack of money has called in to question the ability of Super League to run the game internationally.
But Super League officials are denying such suggestions.

This follows complaints made by the British Lions team manager, Phil Lowe, that his squad is living from hand to mouth. Lowe says neither the Great Britain nor New Zealand leagues have provided money for the tour, and he hasn't been able to pay the players.
Super League's media office in Sydney says the tour was arranged before the formation of Super League's new international board and doesn't reflect its ability to organise the game.
